A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Bongard-RWR+ benchmark and generation pipeline. Their main texts, algorithms, tables, figures, and appendices are readable and support reliable comparison, including matching relocated and renumbered material.

before.justification: v1 reports original model evaluations, concept-generation scores, ablations, and repeated supervised-baseline experiments in Section 4 and Appendix B.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds proprietary-model evaluations, image-contamination experiments, and analyses of annotation reliability and demographic bias.

M1.justification: Algorithms 1–2, the Pixtral-12B/Flux.1-dev pipeline, Similarity Classifier rule, and six task formulations are retained. Expanded annotation documentation does not establish an implemented algorithm change. Cycle-consistency verification and property-based filtering are proposed as future work.

E1.justification: v2 adds Bongard-RWR+/L2-Impure, introducing concept-violating context images as a distinct evaluation condition. It also audits 800 human-depicting images for demographic attributes. The original benchmark concepts, task formulations, and existing dataset variants remain.

E2.justification: Appendix C.11 adds Claude Sonnet 4.5, Gemini 2.5 Pro, and GPT 5.1 to the I1S, D1S, and CS comparisons, substantially extending evaluation to proprietary frontier models. Figure 18 and Tables 14–15 report their participation; the earlier open-model, Similarity Classifier, and supervised baselines are retained.

E3.justification: Added protocols include replacing one image per side with a rejected image in L2-Impure, dividing matrices into three equally sized diversity bins, and independently labeling 800 human images for the bias audit. Existing train/validation/test splits, decoding temperature, and K/P sweeps remain unchanged. The proprietary evaluation is described only as limited.

E4.justification: v2 adds diversity-stratified performance, controlled image-contamination tests, per-concept real/generated-image comparisons, a Similarity Classifier case study, and detailed model failure analyses. Appendix E additionally examines demographic composition, annotation disagreements, and image-rejection patterns. These substantially extend v1's existing ablations and qualitative analyses.

E5.justification: Statistical validation expands beyond v1's supervised-baseline mean and standard deviation reporting. v2 introduces Pearson correlations and fitted-regression statistics for real/generated performance in Table 4, plus Cohen's kappa for filtering and demographic annotations in Appendix E. The existing ten-seed baseline protocol is retained; no increase in repetitions is established.

E6.justification: Matched original benchmark tables retain their scores, but substantial new results appear. Figure 18 reports Gemini 2.5 Pro at 0.82 CS, 0.70 D1S, and 0.65 I1S; Figure 10 reports InternVL2.5 CS accuracy of 0.50 versus 0.62 in low- versus high-diversity bins. Contamination, correlation, annotation-agreement, rejection-rate, and demographic findings are also newly reported.

T1.justification: Section 4 newly defines a matrix-level diversity score: the negative of the larger maximum pairwise cosine similarity across the two sides. This extends the earlier use of similarity for subset selection into an explicit evaluation measure. Existing mathematical task definitions and algorithms remain unchanged, with no new theorems or proofs.

C1.justification: The contribution list qualifies the pipeline as semi-automated rather than automated and specifies limitations in multi-image AVR rather than AVR generally. These are modest scope qualifications; the 5,400-matrix benchmark contribution and central claim about difficulty recognizing fine-grained concepts remain intact.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations for the Similarity Classifier's behavior, specific model failure mechanisms, filtering benefits, and demographic limitations. It also develops future verification strategies and argues that generated-image performance improvements should transfer reliably to real-image problems. This considerably expands v1's interpretation and applicability discussion.

D1.justification: Appendix E.2 newly documents two independent reviewers, Left/Right/None labels, disagreement resolution, and exclusion criteria. Dataset and code links move to project-organization addresses, and v2 states an additional restriction concerning high-stakes human assessment. Existing algorithms, prompts, hardware information, and inference settings are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Wüst et al. on Bongard evaluation, Shukla et al. on generative-model bias, and several works supporting cross-cultural reasoning discussion. These extend the surrounding context without substantially changing the benchmark's positioning. Publication and bibliographic updates to existing references do not constitute new research coverage.

P1.justification: Much of the original prose and main-section sequence is retained. v2 tightens passages, reorders appendices, moves data/code information into a main-text Reproducibility paragraph, and adds dedicated ethics, fairness, and language-model-use sections. These are localized editorial and organizational changes rather than a wholesale rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 adds diversity, contamination, classifier-example, failure-case, proprietary-model, and audit displays in Figures 10, 13, and 15–21, plus Tables 4 and 16. Existing concept-ranking tables gain proprietary-model rows, Figure 5 adds random-guess markers, and the document adopts ICLR formatting. Earlier example figures are retained and relocated, not newly introduced.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's less quantified validation, v2 improves transparency through annotation audits, contamination tests, failure analysis, and frontier-model comparisons. Gains are tempered by limited proprietary-evaluation protocol detail and a transfer claim that correlations across four K settings do not establish. New reporting inconsistencies also remain: Appendix C.9 gives a D1S range of 70–182 solved instances, whereas Figure 16 shows 75–176. The net improvement is useful but limited.
